_meta.probe: P5 — would a diversity term improve what the hook injects?
_meta.verdict: REFUTED. MMR is monotonically worse than plain top-k-by-score.
_meta.reading: Redundancy fell exactly as designed (0.053 -> 0.006) while the useful-line rate fell with it (22.3% -> 15.1%). That is the failure the adoption threshold was written to catch: a metric that improved and a system that did not.
_meta.correction: This also narrows the finding that motivated it. real-usage-report §3 showed the >=0.70 score BAND had 0% reuse and read that as 'score does not predict usefulness'. P5 shows that within a candidate POOL, score predicts usefulness better than novelty does. Those are different questions and the earlier write-up conflated them. Across injections, a high band score means the memory restated the prompt. Within one injection, the highest-scoring candidates are still the best available.
_meta.headroom: The oracle reaches 40.5% against the current 22.3%, so ~18pp of headroom exists and a better selector is possible. It is not MMR over lexical overlap.
method_limits: Pools are RECONSTRUCTED by re-running retrieval against today's DB with the original prompt, because the transcript records only the five lines injected, never the pool. The corpus has changed since; memories written after an injection are ones the hook could never have picked.
Same injections that produced the hypothesis: consistency, not validation.
'Useful' is >=2 distinctive tokens reappearing in later assistant text — token overlap, not comprehension.
